title: Unit Conversion I
statement:
Units come in `n` kinds, labelled `0` to `n - 1`. Each of the `n - 1` entries `conversions[i] = [sourceUnit_i, targetUnit_i, conversionFactor_i]` says that one unit of kind `sourceUnit_i` is worth exactly `conversionFactor_i` units of kind `targetUnit_i`. Starting at kind `0` and applying conversions only from source to target, every other kind can be reached, and in exactly one way: the conversions form a tree rooted at kind `0` whose links all point away from the root.

Return an array of length `n` whose entry `i` is the number of units of kind `i` that one unit of kind `0` is worth (so entry `0` is `1`). These numbers can be enormous, so give each one modulo `10^9 + 7`.
constraints: Applying conversions forward from unit 0 reaches every unit in exactly one way
notes:
## Intuition

Read each conversion as an arrow from `sourceUnit` to `targetUnit` labelled with its factor. Since unit 0 reaches every unit along exactly one forward path, the arrows form a tree hanging from unit 0, and a unit's answer is the product of the factors on its path. A child's amount is therefore its parent's amount times the factor between them, so a breadth-first search from unit 0 fills in every amount from its parent's in one pass. Multiplying out each unit's whole path separately (the brute force) costs O(n) per unit, O(n²) on a long chain.

## Approach

1. Build `children`: for each unit, the `[next, factor]` pairs of the conversions leaving it, with the factor as a BigInt.
2. Set `amount[0] = 1` and start the queue with unit 0.
3. Take the next `unit` from the queue. For each child `next`, set `amount[next] = amount[unit] * factor` modulo 10^9 + 7 and queue `next`.
4. When the queue is used up, every unit has its amount; return them as ordinary numbers.

Every unit other than 0 is the target of exactly one conversion, so it is queued once and no visited set is needed.

## Example 1, step by step

`conversions = [[0,1,2],[1,2,3]]` gives `children[0] = [[1, 2]]` and `children[1] = [[2, 3]]`. The queue starts as `[0]` with `amount = [1, 0, 0]`. Expanding unit 0 sets `amount[1] = 1 * 2 = 2`; expanding unit 1 sets `amount[2] = 2 * 3 = 6`; unit 2 has no children. The answer is `[1, 2, 6]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each conversion is read once to build `children` and once during the search.
- Space: O(n) for `children`, `amount` and the queue.

## Pitfalls

- An amount below 10^9 + 7 times a factor up to 10^9 can reach about 10^18, far past the 2^53 a JavaScript number holds exactly. Multiply as BigInt (`long` in Java and C) before taking the remainder.
- Take the remainder after every multiplication, not once at the end.
- Conversions arrive in any order, so a child can be listed before its parent. One pass over the list in input order may read an amount that is not known yet; the queue expands parents first.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | 10^9 + 7 as a BigInt |
| `n` | number of unit kinds |
| `children` | for each unit, its `[next, factor]` conversions |
| `amount` | units of each kind that one unit of kind 0 is worth, modulo `MOD` |
| `queue`, `head` | the search queue and the index of the next unit to expand |
| `unit`, `next`, `factor` | the unit being expanded, one of its children and the factor between them |

narration.2: Amounts are kept modulo 10^9 + 7; as a BigInt it keeps the product of two large numbers exact.
narration.3: There is one more unit kind than there are conversions.
narration.4: children[u] will list the conversions that start at unit u.
narration.6: ...and file it under its source as [target, factor], with the factor as a BigInt.
narration.9: amount[u] will hold how many units of kind u one unit of kind 0 is worth.
narration.10: One unit of kind 0 is worth exactly one unit of kind 0.
narration.11: The breadth-first search starts at unit 0, the root of the tree.
narration.12: Expand queued units in order; head points at the next one.
narration.13: This unit's amount is already final, because it was set before the unit was queued.
narration.14: Look at every conversion leaving this unit.
narration.15: A child is worth its parent's amount times the factor between them, reduced modulo 10^9 + 7.
narration.16: Queue the child so that its own children are filled in later.
narration.19: Every unit was reached exactly once; return the amounts as ordinary numbers.
